https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The airline said in a memo that the move would reassure passengers and stakeholders By Lauren Turner Published 2 hours ago Air India is to test all of its pilots for banned substances, starting immediately. It comes after an incident last week in which its Phuket to Delhi flight suddenly lost altitude, with a preliminary report saying the senior pilot had to retake their substance test. Reports say they had tested positive for marijuana. Pilots at the airline's budget arm, Air India Express, will also be subject to the tests from Thursday. Existing rules require at least 10% of pilots to be tested at random. Seventeen passengers and crew were injured when the Airbus lost about 91 metres (300 feet) in height shortly after departure on 4 August. It is being investigated by Indian authorities working alongside Airbus and France's air safety agency. Both pilots of the flight have been removed from duties until the investigation is complete. In a memo seen by the BBC, Air India said it was "important to go further" in its testing. "This initiative, which goes beyond regulatory requirements, reflects our determination to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism, and to provide reassurance to our passengers, stakeholders and the community at large," it said. The airline has already been under scrutiny after a June 2025 flight from Ahmedabad to London crashed shortly after take-off, killing 241 people on board and 19 on the ground. Only one passenger survived. The tests - for substances as well as medications prohibited under aviation regulations - are being carried out alongside training sessions at Air India's academy, as well as other locations including briefing centres and offices. Last week, former Ethiopian Airlines boss Tewolde Gebremariam became Air India's new chief executive. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A refugee supper club has been praised as a 'blueprint' for churches across London. The Reverend Rod Green, Bishop of Stepney, made the comments during a visit to the Haven Supper Club, which brings together refugees, asylum seekers and residents at Church on the Corner in Islington for food, music and conversation. Reverend Green said: "Seeing members of the church here serving the local community where they are – this is what the church is about. "It’s wonderful to meet people from all over the world in one room and you can feel the real affection and loyalty people have towards each other. Read more Spa & Massage opens ninth location in Islington Bishop praises refugee supper club as a blueprint for London churches Arsenal’s attacking dynamics still a problem against Brighton "Church on the Corner provides a fantastic blueprint that churches across London can replicate in their own communities." Each month, the club welcomes around 40 to 50 guests for a home-cooked meal and creative activities. The event is organised by Church on the Corner and led by minister Reverend Idina Dunmore and Fergus Burnett-Skelding. It aims to reduce isolation, support integration, and build friendships within the community. At this month’s gathering, guests enjoyed a Mediterranean meal and took part in a group art project exploring themes of migration and journeys. The evening also featured live music from the Romany Diamonds, a family band from the Polish-Romany community who performed traditional folk songs. Past events have included music from Iranian and Congolese artists. Charity Events Leisure Religion Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... The PISA tests: an image of a generation? In the latest PISA tests, Romania ranked third from the bottom in the European Union Photo: pixabay.com Roxana Vasile , 30.09.2026, 13:30 PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment) is the most extensive international educational assessment, a comparative study launched by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to measure the core skills of 15-year-old students in three main areas: Reading, Mathematics, and Science. In addition to measuring student competencies, PISA collects information on educational practices in participating countries and generates high-quality indicators that enable cross-country comparisons and support necessary reforms in their education systems. In Romania, 10,000 students aged 15 from approximately 320 schools and high schools across both urban and rural areas took part in the PISA 2025 tests, the results of which were made public early this autumn. Compared to previous years, the results indicate relatively stable performance in Science and Maths, but a sharp decline in Reading. In Maths, only 48% of Romanian students reached the minimum baseline level (compared to the OECD average of 65%); in Reading, the figure was 52% (compared to the OECD average of 69%); and in Science 54% (compared to the OECD average of 74%). At the other end of the spectrum, the proportion of high-performing Romanian students stayed extremely low: just 4% in Mathematics, 2% in Science, and 1% in Reading. PISA 2025 data also confirmed a stark socio-economic disparity, with disadvantage heavily concentrated in rural schools. Indeed, according to the OECD, Romania ranks among the top 10 countries out of more than 90 where inequality between schools is highest. Speaking to Radio Romania, professor Marian Staş, an education expert and head of the “Third Millennium Leaders Club” Association, believes that taking PISA tests into account is absolutely essential: Marian Staş: “Obviously, it is not the grades, the rankings, or the position itself that matter: after all, we don’t go to school just to look good in PISA! However, PISA is a consequence, an effect of a very, very, very deep-seated cause: the fundamental failure of the Romanian school system to align with the realities of the 21st Century.” The verdict is rather harsh, yet grounded. Although a variety of reforms have been implemented in the Romanian education system over the past four decades or so, few have been effective: Marian Staş: “Unfortunately, as far as we are concerned, functional illiteracy, i.e. reading without grasping the meaning or understanding the text, and mathematical illiteracy are symptoms of a much deeper issue: the fact that schools are, in fact, actively fostering widespread logical illiteracy. These children do not learn to think in school; their minds are not opened. Statistically speaking, there is a lack of educational components or processes designed to open their minds, to help them distinguish cause from effect, understand how to interpret information, and so on… If I were being cynical, I would say the country wants you to be stupid, and I mean that literally. I am not joking when I say it is a hellish combination of trade unionism, imposture, political incompetence, and flawed public policies…” A poorly designed system also entails huge socio-economic and demographic disparities and inequalities, as well as imbalances in resource allocation across different environments: urban, small-town, rural, and so on. How can this situation be addressed then, according to Marian Staş, an education expert and head of the “Third Millennium Leaders Club” Association? Marian Staş: “If you were to ask me how we could do things differently, the two essential interventions would be these: one from within, namely redesigning and structurally transforming the school system itself, and the second, transforming Romania’s administrative-territorial architecture. It is impossible for 21st-Century Romania to work efficiently at all levels with an administrative-territorial map designed 50 years ago. How can it still be valid and yield good results in the economy, healthcare, education, infrastructure, and so on? For God’s sake, this is 2026, the 21st century.” Without genuine, deep-seated reforms, can today’s 15-year-olds reach a level that enables them to meet the demands of the labour market in the years to come? For Marian Staș, the answer is “no”: Marian Staş: “Can they become skilled professionals? No, of course not. Sure, 1, 2, 3, or 5% might, but 90% won’t, because they aren’t getting the right kind of schooling. Healthcare heals and Defence protects, but Education is, by definition, the sole generator of human resources, of whatever quality.” In a word, PISA tests serve as an extremely important academic and social barometer. They indicate whether a generation is equipped with the fundamental intellectual tools required to compete in the labour market. However, it is equally true that these tests cannot define the full human, cultural, or social potential of the young people being assessed, in other words, the “state of a generation.” A generation is far more than just literacy, mathematical, and scientific skills; it is defined by culture, values, emotional intelligence, and adaptability, and these qualities lie beyond the scope of standardised tests. Photograph: Firas Abdullah/Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Firefighters tackled a blaze in Paris as protesters march in the background, 17 October 2026. Photograph: Firas Abdullah/Anadolu/Getty Images Opinion France After the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le Pen Paul Taylor The far-right leader’s promise to restore order will appeal to many ahead of next year’s presidential elections – the stakes are suddenly much higher Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.59 EDT Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.35 EDT Share T here is only one clear winner so far from France’s chaos: Marine Le Pen. The violence and rioting that engulfed towns and cities across the country over the weekend, six months before a pivotal presidential election, is a godsend for the hard-right, Eurosceptical, anti-immigration candidate. As buildings burned , shops were looted and police attacked, the rioting largely drowned out peaceful mass protests over the dilapidated state of schools , fuel prices and the cost of living. Across France and the rest of Europe, people are in shock at scenes of arson and pillage in city centres, the wrecking of symbols of the republic such as the 19th-century town hall in peaceful provincial Limoges and the bust of Marianne in Marseille’s city hall, and the looting of more than 2,000 shops. Though France has a long revolutionary tradition , this was not the work of egalitarian insurgents or working-class warriors, but nihilist, anarchist “black bloc” gangs, with opportunist looters and rioters along for the ride. Emmanuel Macron is a lame-duck president who has no practical answers to a crisis that is ruining his legacy. Macron expressed his “anger and shame” at the violence and the damage to France’s global image in a Sunday-night broadcast to the nation, but he is so widely loathed, including by many who voted for him in two presidential elections, that his pleas for order and dialogue were largely ignored. Le Pen, in contrast, issued a solemn video message , looking presidential as she sat at a desk with the national tricolor (but no EU flag) and bookshelves as her backdrop. Millions of suffering French people were angry about “anarchic immigration” and the cost of living without smashing or burning anything, she said. They would have an opportunity in six months’ time to vote for a different path of “restored authority and security”. Macron’s minority government is trapped in a vicious circle. France’s debt and deficit squeeze leaves him no spare cash left to buy off protesters. A decade of his centre-right presidency has failed to reform a bloated public sector or improve public services. The country has a youth crisis, characterised by anxiety over an economically uncertain future and amplified by social media, as well as a geopolitical crisis with Russia’s war on Ukraine spreading into a covert war against Europe . Foreign critics of progressive European social policies are fanning the flames with incendiary commentaries. Donald Trump gloated on social media that “France is burning!”. Blaming the situation on immigration, he urged the French to “close your borders and take control before it is too late”. Vladimir Putin’s close aide Kirill Dmitriev described events in France as “the suicidal fall of Europe” and also ascribed it in part to chaotic migration. The convergence of crises leaves little room for manoeuvre for a French government struggling to push even a mildly cost-cutting budget through a hung parliament. For now, it is trying to extinguish the violence with selective curfews . One presidential hopeful, Dominique de Villepin, who was a Gaullist prime minister 20 years ago, has even compared the situation to the eve of the fall of the ancien regime in 1788, a year before the outbreak of the Revolution, when France was stricken by drought, failed harvests and empty state coffers. That may be a far-fetched parallel. But the sense of a fraying state, a discredited political class and an ossified bureaucracy unable to staunch a slow-motion financial crisis that might suddenly accelerate makes the stakes in next year’s presidential race ever-higher. Until last weekend’s explosion, the school and student protests, unrest over the cost of living and outrage at instances of police brutality against young demonstrators all seemed to be lifting the campaign of radical-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who in some opinion polls had overtaken the centrist Edouard Philippe for second place. However, Mélenchon’s apparent refusal to clearly condemn the looting or attacks on the police, and his belittling of the violence as “disorder that is part of the events in the life of a society”, may cost him support among more moderate leftwing voters who have boosted Socialist candidate Raphaël Glucksmann in the latest opinion surveys. Investors are taking fright at the violence and political instability, selling French stocks and bonds. A deepening market run on France could yet change the dynamics of the presidential campaign, rallying a frightened middle-class behind a seasoned centrist candidate seen as a safe pair of hands in a crisis. A month after the May 1968 student-worker uprising that rocked Charles de Gaulle’s staid regime, voters scared by the spectre of civil unrest delivered a landslide victory to his party, which promised to restore order and authority. A year later, De Gaulle was disavowed in a referendum on regional devolution and resigned. Historical comparisons are risky. Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy. Economics is Le Pen’s weak spot. So far, neither Philippe nor other centrist and centre-right rivals have set the campaign alight. But six months is a long time in French politics.
